objective: Add provider-neutral fail-closed tool invocation admission that binds resource/audience, exact tool descriptors, scopes, actor, argument digest, risk confirmation, generation, expiry, use limits, replay, and non-authority boundaries without executing tools or handling credentials.

research_inputs.finding: Current frontier tool-use systems add native computer use, configurable confirmation policies, agentic tool calling, and tool search for large tool ecosystems; tool search reduces context overhead but model-selected actions remain untrusted.
research_inputs.implementation_impact: FAISAL adds explicit resource, descriptor, scope, risk, confirmation, and argument-digest admission independent of model capability or tool-search behavior.

research_inputs.finding: Browser pages, documents, ads, and dynamic content are adversarial inputs; even strong models are not immune to prompt injection, so classifier and red-team defenses do not replace execution-layer authorization.
research_inputs.implementation_impact: Tool descriptions/annotations and model outputs remain explicitly untrusted and cannot authorize invocation.

research_inputs.finding: Current MCP authorization guidance uses OAuth 2.1 conventions, Protected Resource Metadata, resource indicators/audience checks, scopes, consent, and server-side validation; it warns against token passthrough.
research_inputs.implementation_impact: FAISAL binds exact resource URI, tool descriptor digest, scope subset, actor, confirmation digest, generation, expiry, and use limits.

research_inputs.finding: MCP safety guidance treats tool descriptions and annotations as untrusted unless trusted by policy and treats tools as arbitrary code/data access paths requiring explicit consent.
research_inputs.implementation_impact: The contract requires annotations_untrusted=true and treats the grant/receipt as evidence rather than production authority.

features: requested scope subset of grant and descriptor

limitations: The contract admits an invocation receipt but never executes a tool, handles OAuth credentials, introspects tokens, or performs external resource authorization.
Resource URI, descriptor digest, scopes, risk, confirmation digest, and actor identity are caller-supplied evidence and require an external identity/authorization provider for production trust.
A matching confirmation digest proves only linkage of supplied evidence; it does not prove a human approved the action unless an independent operator system attests it.
The benchmark measures local Python receipt overhead and excludes OAuth, network, browser, tool, accelerator, storage, and kernel latency.
The real held-out evaluation uses deterministic fixture adapters and does not measure tool authorization quality, browser autonomy, robotics, frontier models, or general intelligence.
No physical accelerator, TPM, secure enclave, production KMS, independent builder, live multihost deployment, or external security review was exercised.
This evidence does not claim AGI capability, production approval, superiority to Linux, or closure of existing external release blockers.
